metaDescription: The working vocabulary of the Nervous System & Authorship framework: regulation, capacity, load, the zones, clean desire, containment, co-regulation, and more.
heading: Glossary and orientation guide
lede: These are the terms the framework uses, and they are used precisely. Most of them are ordinary words carrying a specific meaning here, which is exactly why they are worth defining.
standfirst: If you read nothing else on this site, this page is a reasonable place to start.

terms.definition: The ability to move flexibly between activation and rest while maintaining agency and connection. Regulation is not calmness — it is adaptability.
Your current ability to tolerate stimulation, emotion, intensity, connection, stress, or uncertainty without losing agency. Capacity fluctuates daily.

The total physiological and psychological demand currently placed on your system. Sleep debt, conflict, secrecy, shame, travel, pressure, illness — all of it adds up. Capacity minus load determines what you can metabolise.
Choosing from present regulation rather than defending a fixed self-concept.
Regulated, open, flexible. Voluntary engagement, connection, and learning are most available here.
Rising activation. Vigilance increasing. Narrative forming. Control impulses appearing. The zone where a small intervention does the most good.
Overwhelm, shutdown, impulsivity, or threat-dominant behaviour. Not a failure state — a signal that capacity has been exceeded and restoration is needed.
Inputs that lower arousal and increase the sense of safety: warmth, slow touch, quiet walking, sunlight, gentle breath, safe conversation. Best when you are safety-seeking or overloaded.

Inputs that raise arousal in a structured, contained way: intense exercise, sexual expression, creative performance, debate, surfing, cold exposure. Healthy when capacity is high; disregulating when load is already high.
Selecting activating or non-activating inputs based on your current state. Regulation is not about calming down — it is about matching stimulation to capacity.
Present-moment wanting that does not require control, fantasy, outcome, or reassurance in order to survive. It is stable, and it does not spike or collapse dramatically.
Future-oriented activation fuelled by projection and imagined possibility, often mistaken for desire. It feels intense, and it tends to collapse the moment obligation appears.
The psychological and nervous-system load that arises when interacting with unfamiliar people. The system enters a mild state of vigilance, which increases cognitive load and emotional activation.
A pattern in which desire diminishes once expectation, exclusivity pressure, or demand enters the system. The nervous system shifts from voluntary engagement to compliance threat.
Prematurely judging present behaviour through imagined future criticism or identity preservation. A regulatory strategy disguised as morality.
The ability to hold activation without impulsively escalating, suppressing, or collapsing. Metabolised intensity.
Stabilisation through safe relational contact. Human nervous systems regulate one another; this is not a workaround for weak self-regulation.
The felt sense that you can leave, pause, or stop without coercion. It increases safety, and it preserves desire.
The ability to explore multiple relational trajectories without premature exclusivity or guilt.
Mutual pull toward connection that does not require force.
The frequency and availability of meaningful social interactions within a given environment — the likelihood that weak social ties will form and gradually deepen into friendship or relationship.
When a neutral sensation or a simple desire is rapidly layered with identity-based narrative. Clean desire suffocates under excessive meaning.
Behaviour driven by perception control rather than by authentic desire.
The regulatory cost of holding information that cannot be integrated safely.
A structured model in three tiers, designed to protect against chronic yellow-zone living.

tiers.name: Fulfilment
tiers.body: Present-moment joy that is not tied to productivity.
